verses.1: Samaria will be destroyed, for she has rebelled against her God. The sword will strike down her people and tear open their children’s wombs. Her strongholds will be shattered.
verses.2: Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled in your sins.
verses.3: Take with you words and return to the LORD. Say to him, "Take away all guilt, and give us good things, and we will offer the fruit of our lips."
verses.4: Assyria will not save us, we will not ride a warhorse, and we will no longer say, “Our gods are the works of our hands,” for in you the orphan finds compassion.
verses.5: I will heal their brokenness and love them freely, for my anger has turned away from them.
verses.6: I will be like the dew to Israel — he will blossom like the lily, and his roots will take hold like Lebanon.
verses.7: His branches will grow, and he will bear fruit like the olive, and his fragrance will be like Lebanon.
verses.8: Those living under his shade will return, they will revive in grain and flourish like the vine. His memory will be like wine, the aroma of Lebanon.
verses.9: What more is there for you, O Ephraim, to seek idols? I have afflicted you, I will yet subdue you. I am like a mother bear in labor — your fruit is found in me.
verses.10: Who is wise and will understand these things? Who is discerning and will know them? The ways of the LORD are upright, and the righteous will walk in them, but the wicked will stumble in them.

notes:
Notes
- v. 1: “The sword will strike down her people and tear open their children’s wombs” is a literal rendering of the Hebrew, which is a poetic but graphic expression of divine judgment.
- v. 9: “I am like a mother bear in labor” reflects the Hebrew metaphor but is rendered in natural English phrasing. The Septuagint uses the metaphor of a bear differently, but the Hebrew supports the interpretation as a mother bear in labor.
raw:
[1] Samaria will be destroyed, for she has rebelled against her God. The sword will strike down her people and tear open their children’s wombs. Her strongholds will be shattered.

[2] Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled in your sins.

[3] Take with you words and return to the LORD. Say to him, "Take away all guilt, and give us good things, and we will offer the fruit of our lips."

[4] Assyria will not save us, we will not ride a warhorse, and we will no longer say, “Our gods are the works of our hands,” for in you the orphan finds compassion.

[5] I will heal their brokenness and love them freely, for my anger has turned away from them.

[6] I will be like the dew to Israel — he will blossom like the lily, and his roots will take hold like Lebanon.

[7] His branches will grow, and he will bear fruit like the olive, and his fragrance will be like Lebanon.

[8] Those living under his shade will return, they will revive in grain and flourish like the vine. His memory will be like wine, the aroma of Lebanon.

[9] What more is there for you, O Ephraim, to seek idols? I have afflicted you, I will yet subdue you. I am like a mother bear in labor — your fruit is found in me.

[10] Who is wise and will understand these things? Who is discerning and will know them? The ways of the LORD are upright, and the righteous will walk in them, but the wicked will stumble in them.

---
Notes
- v. 1: “The sword will strike down her people and tear open their children’s wombs” is a literal rendering of the Hebrew, which is a poetic but graphic expression of divine judgment.
- v. 9: “I am like a mother bear in labor” reflects the Hebrew metaphor but is rendered in natural English phrasing. The Septuagint uses the metaphor of a bear differently, but the Hebrew supports the interpretation as a mother bear in labor.
